intro: A willow oak at Bonny Oaks, on the north-east side of Chattanooga, was already standing when an orphanage opened on the farm around it in 1854, by the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council's account. It grows in a small round arboretum of 55 species in front of the Dent House, built in 1840, and the arboretum is free and open every day, about 10 miles from downtown. If you know another old tree in Chattanooga worth the walk, tell us.
meta_description: The Bonny Oaks Willow Oak in Chattanooga, a registered Historic Tree said to predate the 1854 Bonny Oaks Orphanage, in a free arboretum.
question_meta: The Bonny Oaks Willow Oak predates the 1854 Bonny Oaks Orphanage, says the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council, which makes it over 170 years old.
question_answer: The Bonny Oaks Willow Oak stands in Bonny Oaks Arboretum at 6183 Adamson Circle, in front of the Dent House on the north-east side of Chattanooga. The Tennessee Urban Forestry Council says it dates from before 1854, which would make it more than 170 years old; Wikipedia says over 100 years and calls it the oldest tree in the arboretum.
question_context: The willow oak at Bonny Oaks has outlasted several owners of the ground it stands on. This was Cherokee land before Colonel Lewis Shepherd settled the area. Colonel Jarrett G. Dent built his house there in 1840, and the Dent House is now on the National Register of Historic Places and serves as the Hamilton County Agriculture Center. In 1854 the Bonny Oaks Orphanage was established on the farm to teach children agricultural skills, and the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council says the willow oak was already growing by then. In 1867 Captain C. C. Peak named the place Bonnie Oaks for the stately oaks around the homestead. The council listed the tree as a Historic Tree in 2000. Sources disagree on its age, from over 100 years in Wikipedia to over 170 by the council's account, and nobody has published its girth or height. The arboretum around it holds 55 species in a small round park on county land, free and open daily. If you go with a tape measure, tell us what you find.

faq.q: Is Bonny Oaks Arboretum free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It is a small round park on Hamilton County Parks land, open daily without charge, in front of the Dent House at 6183 Adamson Circle.

faq.q: How far is the Bonny Oaks Willow Oak from downtown Chattanooga?
faq.a: About 10 miles, on the north-east side of the city near Lake Vista.

trees.story:
The Tennessee Urban Forestry Council says this willow oak was already standing when the Bonny Oaks Orphanage opened in 1854 to teach children farming on a working farm. By the council's reckoning that makes it more than 170 years old. Wikipedia, more cautiously, says over 100 years, and calls it the oldest tree in an arboretum of 55 species.

The ground has changed hands around it. It was Cherokee land before Colonel Lewis Shepherd settled the area. Colonel Jarrett G. Dent built the house behind the tree in 1840, and the Dent House is now on the National Register of Historic Places. In 1867 Captain C. C. Peak named the place Bonnie Oaks for the stately oaks around the homestead. Whether this oak was one of the trees he meant, nobody wrote down.

The council named it a Historic Tree in 2000. The Dent House is now the Hamilton County Agriculture Center, and the arboretum in front of it is a small round park on county land, free and open every day, on the north-east side of Chattanooga about 10 miles from downtown.

Nobody has published its girth or its height. If you go with a tape measure, tell us what you find, and if you know of other old trees in Chattanooga worth the walk, tell us about those too.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its narrow, willow-like leaves, unusual on an oak. It stands in the small round Bonny Oaks Arboretum in front of the Dent House, 6183 Adamson Circle.

trees.access: Free; Bonny Oaks Arboretum is a small round park open daily without charge (Wikipedia). It sits on Hamilton County Parks land.

trees.verify_notes: TUFC register: the willow oak stands in Hamilton County on land once occupied by the Cherokee. Colonel Lewis Shepherd settled the area; Colonel Jarrett G. Dent built the Dent House (National Register) in 1840; Captain C.C. Peak named the place Bonnie Oaks in 1867 for the stately oaks around the homestead. The register says the tree dates to before 1854, when the Bonny Oaks Orphanage was established to teach agrarian skills on a working farm. Historic Tree 2000, nominated by Kelly Jackson. Tree is on Hamilton County Parks property. Age conflict: TUFC says before 1854 (so over about 170 years), Wikipedia describes the willow oak in the arboretum as over 100 years old and the oldest specimen in the 55-species collection. I record the register's date as a lower bound; stated as 'over 170 years' with a flag. The Times Free Press (Dec 2015, a story on the fall of the Baylor red oak) has the city forester calling it one of the few remaining historically significant oaks in the county (that article read via search summary only, not fetched, so that quote is unverified). Pin is the arboretum centre (Nominatim for the address 35.07306,-85.18270), not the trunk: the arboretum is a small round park so a visitor will find the largest oak. Alive: TUFC entry modified 2026-01-22; lifecheck RECENT (iNaturalist 2025-10-13 within 100 m of the arboretum, not tied to this trunk). Photo: none found on Commons by geosearch (250 m).

Sidewalk to Brainerd Road is still a wish-list item per the church. Treat as view from public ground; confirm before relying on entry.

trees.story:
The grounds of Grace Episcopal Church hold 73 kinds of tree, and the two the city singled out are a pair of oaks. A 2022 Chattanooga Times Free Press report called a water oak and a willow oak the oldest and tallest trees on the property, and said both are on Chattanooga's Notable Trees Register.

The rest of the lawn explains why they have so much company. The church turned its roughly four acres into the GreenGrace Arboretum, and in December 2021 the Tennessee Urban Forestry Council certified it as a Level Two arboretum, the grade for a collection of 60 or more species.

Now the limits. The city's register is a map that is not published, and the newspaper article, our main source for the two oaks, no longer loads at its original address. No age, girth or height has been published for either tree, and we cannot tell you which of the two is the willow oak. So treat this as a pair to find rather than a single trunk, and look for the two tallest trees on the grounds.

The church stands on the corner of Brainerd Road and Belvoir Avenue, and its tree-covered lawn can be seen from the street. The arboretum is meant for visitors, but we found no published hours, so if nobody is about, look from the road. If you know these two, or which is which, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two tallest trees on the church grounds, a water oak and a willow oak. They stand on the tree-covered lawn of Grace Episcopal, at Brainerd Road and Belvoir Avenue.
